report.summary: Analyzed shape.py chunk 1: module docstring explains purpose and safety, defines constants, helper functions, Shape dataclass with to_dict/signature/render, and describe function up to TREE branch. Public symbols and claims enumerated.
risks: describe function | medium | The TREE branch uses a for-loop over ("keys",) which is redundant; the loop body always executes once. If intended to iterate over multiple attributes, it's incomplete. | Check if the loop is meant to iterate over more attributes like "keys" and "members".

to_dict | low | The 'n_names' field is omitted when n_names is 0, but if names are present and n_names is 0, it might be ambiguous. | Verify that n_names is always set correctly when names are present.

signature | low | The signature method includes n_names in the bits only if length >= 0, but n_names is independent of length. | Review if signature should include n_names when names are present but length is -1.
todos: Check if the TREE branch loop is intended to cover more attributes (e.g., 'members', 'GetListOfKeys').
Ensure that n_names is always set consistently with names length.
Add tests for edge cases: empty arrays, tables with no columns, objects with missing attributes.

claims.text: A declaration says ``def load(p: str) -> Run``. A checker can sometimes prove a little more. Neither can tell you what you see the moment you stop in a debugger
claims.why: This claim refers to external code (declaration, checker) not present in this chunk.

claims.text: Nothing here reads an element, a cell, a row or a scalar payload.
claims.why: The code in this chunk only accesses attributes like dtype, shape, columns, keys, nbytes, flags, etc. It does not index into the object or read values.

claims.text: a value can be gigabytes, and an observer that copies data is a memory bug;
claims.why: The module avoids reading values; it only accesses metadata attributes.

claims.text: a value can be a secret, and this repo's whole egress posture is built on not moving those;
claims.why: Refers to repo's egress posture, not present in this chunk.

claims.text: the graph does not want the value. It wants the shape.
claims.why: Refers to 'the graph', not defined in this chunk.

claims.text: Even names are not automatically safe — a column called ``patient_id`` is a disclosure. So ``describe`` takes a ``redact`` hook, and the caller that ships an observation anywhere near a model is expected to pass one.
claims.why: The describe function signature includes a redact parameter, and it is called on names in the code (e.g., `red(c) for c in ...`). The claim is consistent with the code.

claims.text: This module owns no policy about what is sensitive; ``daedalus.sensitivity`` does, and the two are kept apart on purpose.
claims.why: Refers to daedalus.sensitivity module, not present in this chunk.

claims.text: Because getting a live object means the program RAN. ``structcore`` is a static pass by construction and ``tools/vet.py`` states the rule outright: you do not run untrusted code to decide anything about it.
claims.why: Refers to structcore and tools/vet.py, not present in this chunk.

claims.text: observation is a separate, opt-in lane that *feeds* the graph with edges stamped ``provenance=observed`` — it is never part of an index build, and it runs only on trees the operator owns.
claims.why: Refers to graph and index build, not present in this chunk.

claims.text: ``(1000, 3)`` is the shape this input produced. It is not the shape the function requires. A field never seen is not a field that cannot appear. Every record carries ``provenance="observed"`` and the run it came from, and any consumer that reports it as a fact is wrong
claims.why: The Shape dataclass has a provenance field defaulting to 'observed'. The claim about shapes being sample-based is reflected in the module's design.

claims.text: Duck-typed throughout: numpy, pandas, h5py and uproot are probed by attribute, never imported. A tree without them degrades to the generic families and says so.
claims.why: The code uses hasattr checks (e.g., hasattr(obj, 'dtype'), hasattr(obj, 'columns'), hasattr(obj, 'keys')) and does not import those libraries. The describe function checks for attributes like 'num_entries' and module names, but does not import.

claims.text: ``_attr``: Attribute or default, WITHOUT using truthiness. ``getattr(obj, "columns", ()) or ()`` looks harmless and raises on a pandas Index, whose ``__bool__`` refuses to answer. Any observer that touches array-likes has to fetch attributes without asking whether they are truthy.
claims.why: The _attr function uses `getattr(obj, name, None)` and then checks `if v is None`, avoiding truthiness checks on the attribute value itself.

claims.text: ``_human_bytes``: Format byte count in human-readable form (B, KiB, etc.).
claims.why: The implementation has a bug: the loop condition `if n < 1024 or unit == "TiB"` is always true for the first iteration (unit == 'B'), so it will always return bytes. The division `n /= 1024.0` happens after the check, but the return uses `n / 1` which is unchanged. It never formats KiB or higher correctly.

claims.text: ``signature``: A stable one-line form, for comparing two observations or joining an observation against a declared type. Deterministic: names are already in a fixed order and nothing here consults a hash seed.
claims.why: The signature method concatenates fields in a fixed order (family, type_name, dtype, dims, names, length). Names are stored as a tuple, preserving order. No hash seed is used.

claims.text: ``render``: The debug-console line this record stands in for.
claims.why: The render method produces a string similar to debugger output, showing type, dtype, dims, layout, bytes, and names.

claims.text: ``_names_of``: Bounded, order-preserving name extraction with the TRUE count kept.
claims.why: The function converts to list (preserving order), clips to MAX_NAMES, returns shown names, total count, and truncation flag.

claims.text: ``describe``: Describe one live object's SHAPE. Never reads a value.
claims.why: The code in this chunk only accesses attributes like dtype, shape, columns, keys, nbytes, flags, etc. It does not read elements.

claims.text: ``redact`` is called on every key/column name before it is stored
claims.why: In the array-like branch: `names, n_names, trunc = _names_of(red(f) for f in fields)`; in the table branch: `names, n_names, trunc = _names_of(red(c) for c in ...)`; in the TREE branch: `names, n_names, trunc = _names_of(red(k) for k in list(obj.keys()))`. The redact function is applied to each name.

observations.what: The _human_bytes function has a bug: it always returns bytes because the loop condition is always true on first iteration and the division happens after the check, but the return uses n/1 which is unchanged.

The describe function's TREE branch uses a for loop over a tuple with a single element ("keys"), which is unnecessary. It may be intended to iterate over multiple attributes like 'keys', 'members', etc., but currently only 'keys' is considered.
The describe function is incomplete in this chunk; it ends in the middle of the TREE branch. The function definition is cut off.
